title: Multiple State Variables and Derived State

subChunks.title: Multiple State Variables and Derived State
subChunks.hookHtml: Every new developer over-uses useState. They create a state variable for every value they track — including values that could simply be calculated from other state. This creates synchronisation bugs: two pieces of state that represent the same truth, drifting apart. The skill is knowing what to put in state vs. what to derive.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Vex: "Ask yourself: can this value be calculated from what I already have? If yes — calculate it. Do not put it in state. State is for values that cannot be derived from anything else."

When to use multiple useState calls

Use separate useState calls for independent values. They don't need to be updated together:

const [username, setUsername] = useState('');
const [email, setEmail] = useState('');
const [age, setAge] = useState(18);

// These three are independent — changing one doesn't affect the others.
// Three separate useState calls is correct here.

When to use one object in useState

Group related values that always change together:

// Good candidate for a single object:
const [position, setPosition] = useState({ x: 0, y: 0 });

// You always update x and y together — one setter is cleaner
function handleMouseMove(e) {
  setPosition({ x: e.clientX, y: e.clientY });
}

Derived state — compute, don't store

If a value can be calculated from existing state or props, compute it inline. Do not put it in useState:

// ❌ Derived state — out of sync risk:
const [items, setItems] = useState([...]);
const [count, setCount] = useState(0); // BUG: must remember to update both!

// ✅ Derived value — always accurate:
const [items, setItems] = useState([...]);
const count = items.length; // Computed on every render from source of truth

// More examples of derived values:
const completedCount = tasks.filter(t => t.done).length;
const totalPrice = cartItems.reduce((sum, item) => sum + item.price * item.qty, 0);
const isFormValid = username.length >= 3 && email.includes('@');
const hasResults = searchResults.length > 0;

The litmus test for state

A value belongs in state if all three are true:

  1. It changes over time in response to user actions or async events
  2. It cannot be calculated from other state or props
  3. React needs to re-render when it changes

If it fails any test — it's not state.

The danger of redundant state

// ❌ firstName, lastName, AND fullName in state:
const [firstName, setFirstName] = useState('');
const [lastName, setLastName] = useState('');
const [fullName, setFullName] = useState(''); // REDUNDANT — must sync manually

// Every update to firstName must also update fullName. You will forget.

// ✅ Derive fullName — always correct, zero maintenance:
const [firstName, setFirstName] = useState('');
const [lastName, setLastName] = useState('');
const fullName = `${firstName} ${lastName}`;

storyBeats.text: Vex draws a map on the workbench — a city district where two scribes track the same census. One updates his scroll, forgets to tell the other. A week later the counts diverge.

storyBeats.speaker: Vex the Interface Weaver
storyBeats.text: Every piece of redundant state is two sources of truth waiting to disagree. You added a count alongside a list — now every list update must also update the count. You will forget once. The bug will be subtle. The fix is simple: don't store what you can calculate.

storyBeats.speaker: State vs derived value

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
Build a cart summary component. State is an array of { id, name, price, qty } objects. Derive all totals — do not store them in state.

  • Render a list of items
  • Render <p data-testid="item-count"> showing the number of unique items
  • Render <p data-testid="total-qty"> showing the sum of all quantities
  • Render <p data-testid="total-price"> showing the total cost (price × qty for each item, summed)
  • Add a <button data-testid="add"> that appends a new item { id: Date.now(), name: 'Potion', price: 5, qty: 1 }

guidedPracticeTests.label: After add, item count updates to 3

subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: Build a <ReadingList> from scratch. State: array of { id, title, read } books. Render the full list. Derive and display (do not store in state): total books, number read, number unread, and percentage read (0 decimal places). A 'Mark Read' button on each unread book sets read: true.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain the concept of derived state to a new React developer. Give three concrete examples where storing an extra piece of state would create a synchronisation bug — and show how calculating the value instead eliminates the bug entirely.

questions.prompt: A value is appropriate for `useState` when:
options: It changes over time, cannot be derived from other state/props, and must trigger a re-render when it changes
It is used in more than one component
It is a number or a boolean (not an array or object)
It is fetched from an API
questions.answer: It changes over time, cannot be derived from other state/props, and must trigger a re-render when it changes
questions.explanation: All three conditions must hold. If a value can be calculated from existing state, it should be derived inline — not stored. If it doesn't need to trigger a re-render, a ref (not state) is appropriate. API data does belong in state, but because it passes the three tests, not simply because it comes from an API.

questions.prompt: A shopping cart has state `items` (array). A developer adds `const [total, setTotal] = useState(0)` and updates it manually on every item change. What is the correct approach?
options: Derive total inline: `const total = items.reduce((s, i) => s + i.price, 0)`
Keep both — total in state for performance, updated with useEffect
Use useCallback to memoize the total calculation
The developer's approach is correct — useState is always better for values displayed in the UI
questions.answer: Derive total inline: `const total = items.reduce((s, i) => s + i.price, 0)`
questions.explanation: Total is a function of items — it can always be recalculated from the source of truth. Storing it separately creates a synchronisation requirement: every items update must also call setTotal. Calculating it inline is always accurate and requires zero maintenance.

questions.prompt: You have `firstName` and `lastName` in state. When should `fullName` be in state rather than derived?
options: Never — fullName can always be derived as `${firstName} ${lastName}`
When fullName can be edited independently of firstName and lastName
When the component re-renders more than 10 times per second
When TypeScript strict mode is enabled
questions.answer: When fullName can be edited independently of firstName and lastName
questions.explanation: If fullName can be edited to something that doesn't match firstName + lastName (e.g. a display alias), then it carries independent information and belongs in state. But if fullName is always just firstName + ' ' + lastName, deriving it is always correct. Only store state when there is information that cannot be reconstructed from other state.
